title: The Sehskriti's warnings
hookLine: wealth, youth and family are passing, it says (Salok Sehskriti)

cards: The word knocks like a hand on a door, again and again. It opens one of Guru Arjan's verses in the Salok Sehskriti, and roughly it asks: where is? who is?
Where is the mother, where is the father, where is the wife, the son? A question asked that many times in a row stops being a question and becomes a drumbeat. Yesterday was the old style.
Today is what that style says, and it's a plain warning.

teach.h: WHO IS MOTHER, WHO IS FATHER?
teach.b: Here's the verse, paraphrased. Who is mother, who is father, who is wife, who are the children you delight in? Who are brother, friend and kin, and what is the pull of the household?

The bright, enchanting beauty of the world: you see it, and it leaves. What stays with you, Nanak says, is the remembrance of the Lord. Put simply, these warnings name three things that pass: wealth, youth, family.
Now a careful note, because this is easy to mishear.

teach.h: NOT A COMMAND TO LEAVE HOME.
teach.b: Sikh teachers don't read it as a command to walk away from family. This path has seen Guru Ram Das build a town and pass the Guruship to his son, and Sikh teaching honors the householder's life.
Katanch isn't asking whether your mother matters. It's asking where she can go with you, in the end, and where you can go with her. The honest answer: not all the way.
Every bond has a door it can't pass through. Some readers hear the verse less as a loss and more as a sorting.

teach.h: ONLY THE NAME GOES ALL THE WAY.
teach.b: Love your people fully, it seems to say, and don't make them carry the weight only the Name can hold.
If a loss is heavy on you right now, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

how: Guru Arjan's Salok Sehskriti are read during a full reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and lines like these are often explained in katha, where gianis set the warnings about passing things beside the Sikh honor for family life.

o: a list of rules about what to give up in a fast
a command to leave your family for a life of prayer
verses saying loved ones and beauty pass; remembrance stays

games.q: inside the warning: tap the pairs.
p: bonds that can't go all the way
you see it, and it leaves

s: the verse tells Sikhs to leave their families
the Gurus were householders; the verse asks where each bond can go with you, not whether it matters.
the verse names what stays when the rest passes
the remembrance of the Lord, Nanak says, stays with you.

games.q: the verse keeps knocking: where is mother, where is father, where is the child? what is it asking?
o: whether your family matters at all.
where each bond can go with you, and what stays to the end.
how to leave home and become an ascetic.
games.why: katanch sorts rather than rejects: love your people fully, and remember that only the Name goes all the way.

practice: Choose something you love that won't last forever: a cup you use every morning, a season, your own strength. Hold it in your mind, or in your hands if it's near, and loosen your grip a little, the way you'd hold a bird.
Be grateful it's here and honest that it passes, and if you pray, let Waheguru ride each breath out.

wordCard.voice: The Sehskriti's warnings. Mother, father, child, the world's bright beauty: they pass, this verse says; the remembrance of the Lord stays. Today's word.

orig.note: where is? who is?: the knocking word that opens Guru Arjan's verse in the Salok Sehskriti.

carryVoice: Your line: passing things. That closes a week of letters and old tongues. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Sehskriti Mahala 5 (katanch mata katanch pita), Ang 1353–1354
